# Deck Visual System Contract

## No brand assets included
This skill ships no brand assets, no company brand guidelines, no colour palette,
and no trademarked type system.
It is a generic restrained editorial system for business decks.
The reader must substitute their own employer's approved fonts, colours, and logo
usage before producing external materials.
The reader must check brand and legal policy before using any logo, including a
customer's logo.
Do not infer, reproduce, or approximate any company's brand system from examples,
slides, screenshots, or memory.
Use this system only as structure, spacing, hierarchy, accessibility, and quality
control guidance.

## Purpose
This skill gives deck agents a consistent visual contract for readable,
credible, vendor-neutral presentations.
It applies to new decks, deck refreshes, executive readouts, enablement material,
and visual QA passes.
The goal is clarity under time pressure, not decoration.

## Required inputs
| Input | Required | Source | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audience | yes | profile, crm, notes | Sets density, detail, and tone. |
| Use context | yes | user, notes, decks | Distinguishes live presentation from leave-behind document. |
| Content outline | yes | user, notes, web, crm | Provides story and evidence. |
| Approved brand choices | conditional | user, decks | Supplies allowed fonts, colours, and logos. |
| Data sources | conditional | crm, web, notes, decks | Supports charts and figures. |
If approved brand choices are missing, use neutral placeholders and tell the
runner to apply approved brand assets before use.

## Core definitions
A slide idea is the single claim the slide exists to prove.
A takeaway title is a sentence that states the conclusion, not the topic.
A safe area is the inner region where text and critical visuals cannot be clipped
by projection, screen sharing, or export.
A display role is the type style for titles, section markers, and major numbers.
A body role is the type style for paragraphs, labels, captions, and speaker cues.
A semantic colour is a colour whose meaning is defined, such as positive,
caution, or negative.

## Typography system
Use a two-role type system: display and body.
Display type carries hierarchy and emphasis.
Body type carries reading, labels, captions, and detail.
Use no more than two type families in a deck.
If the approved brand system uses one family, use weight, size, and spacing to
create hierarchy.
If the approved brand system uses two families, reserve one for display and one
for body.
Do not add decorative fonts.
Do not mix type families because a slide feels empty.

## Relative type scale
Define the body text size as one unit.
Use this ratio-based scale.
| Role | Relative size | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Caption | 0.75x body | Source notes, chart labels, footnotes. |
| Body | 1.00x body | Main reading text. |
| Emphasis | 1.25x body | Short callouts and key labels. |
| Subtitle | 1.60x body | Secondary titles or section context. |
| Title | 2.00x body | Slide takeaway title. |
| Hero | 3.00x body | One number or phrase on a statement slide. |
Keep ratios consistent across the deck.
Never shrink text below readability limits to force content onto a slide.
For a projected slide, body text must be large enough to read from the back of a
meeting room.
As a hard floor, projected body text should not be smaller than twenty four point
equivalent.
For a document sent to read, body text should not be smaller than eleven point
equivalent.
Captions and sources may be smaller, but must remain legible after export.
Limit line length to forty to sixty characters for body text.
Limit slide titles to two lines.
Use line spacing that prevents ascenders and descenders from touching.
Avoid all caps except short labels.

## Colour system
Use a neutral base for most surfaces, text, rules, and containers.
Use one accent colour sparingly for emphasis, navigation, or the primary action.
Use a defined semantic set for meaning.
| Semantic role | Meaning | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Positive | Progress, improvement, health | Status, trend, or confirmed benefit. |
| Caution | Risk, watch item, uncertainty | Items needing attention. |
| Negative | Loss, blocker, decline, breach | Confirmed problem or missed threshold. |
| Neutral | Context, baseline, unknown | Background and comparison. |
Colour must never be the only carrier of meaning.
Pair colour with text, icon shape, line pattern, position, or label.
Meet a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 for normal text.
Meet a contrast ratio of at least 3 to 1 for large text, icons, and meaningful
chart marks.
Do not use low-contrast grey text for important content.
Do not use red and green alone to distinguish states.
Avoid gradients unless they encode data and remain accessible.

## Layout grid
Use one grid throughout the deck.
A twelve-column grid is preferred because it supports halves, thirds, and
quarters.
Use consistent outer margins on every slide.
Keep critical content inside the safe area.
Use a larger top region for the takeaway title and a stable footer region for
sources or navigation.
Align objects to the grid unless intentional overlap explains a relationship.
Use whitespace as a grouping tool.
Do not fill whitespace with decoration.

## Named layouts
| Layout | Correct use | Required elements |
|---|---|---|
| Title | Opening the deck or a major conversation | Clear deck purpose, audience context, date or version if needed. |
| Statement | Landing one executive point | One takeaway sentence or one hero metric with source. |
| Two-column comparison | Showing choices, before and after, or trade-offs | Balanced headings, matched units, explicit conclusion. |
| Data with takeaway | Answering a quantitative question | Takeaway title, chart, source, unit, period, and note on caveats. |
| Sequence or timeline | Showing order, dependency, maturity, or plan | Steps, owners if known, timing, and current position. |
| Section divider | Resetting the story between chapters | Short section claim, not a decorative pause. |
| Closing ask | Ending with a decision or next step | Clear ask, owner, timing, and consequence of no action. |
Do not create a new layout until one of these cannot express the idea.
Repeated layouts should preserve placement of title, source, and primary content.

## Content discipline
One slide gets one idea.
The title states the takeaway, not the topic.
No chart is allowed without its takeaway in the title.
No slide should be only a list of nouns.
Every bullet must have a verb, implication, or decision relevance.
Use slide notes for detail that does not need to be seen.
For live delivery, plan roughly one slide per two minutes.
For executive readouts, use fewer slides and stronger titles.
For leave-behind documents, allow more detail but preserve hierarchy and sources.
If a slide needs more than three visual groups, split it.
If the presenter must apologize for density, split it.

## Data visuals
Choose chart type by the question asked.
| Question | Preferred visual |
|---|---|
| How much or how many | Bar, column, or single-number statement. |
| How has it changed over time | Line chart or small multiples. |
| How do parts compare to a whole | Stacked bar when categories are few, otherwise table. |
| Where is the exception | Ranked bar, highlight table, or annotated scatter. |
| What is the sequence | Timeline, process flow, or dependency map. |
| What are the trade-offs | Two-column comparison or decision matrix. |
Start bar charts at zero.
Label every axis with unit and period.
Use direct labels instead of legends when space allows.
If a legend is required, keep categories few and order the legend like the data.
Every figure carries its source.
Every metric identifies its time period.
Do not use three-dimensional charts.
Do not use pie charts when precise comparison matters.
Do not crop axes to exaggerate change.
Do not mix units on one axis.

## Image and icon rules
Use images only when they carry information or emotional context that the words
cannot carry alone.
Do not use decorative stock imagery with no informational role.
Use icons sparingly and consistently.
An icon must label, group, or clarify an idea.
Do not create icon soup.
If an icon needs a paragraph to explain it, remove it.
Check image rights and brand policy before use.
Customer logos require permission or an approved usage basis.

## Source and evidence rules
Every figure, quote, benchmark, and customer claim needs a visible source or a
speaker note source.
Use source names from crm, workplace, notes, web, or decks.
Do not cite inaccessible evidence in an external deck.
Do not expose confidential source details.
If evidence cannot be shown, either generalize the claim or remove it.

## Visual QA checklist
Run this checklist before a deck is done.
1. No text, chart, table, logo, or shape overflows or clips after export.
2. Text and meaningful visuals meet contrast thresholds.
3. Type families, sizes, weights, and spacing are consistent.
4. Margins, safe area, title position, and footer position are consistent.
5. No orphaned or widowed text creates awkward single-word lines.
6. Every figure, benchmark, quote, and claim has a source.
7. No placeholder text, placeholder icon, or draft label remains.
8. Capitalization is consistent across titles, labels, and bullets.
9. Images are sharp enough for projection and export.
10. Logos, if any, follow approved brand and legal policy.
11. Colour is not the only carrier of meaning.
12. Every slide title states a takeaway.
13. Every chart has a visible unit and period.
14. Slide density varies with the story and does not feel uniform.
15. The closing slide has a clear ask or decision.
If any check fails, fix the deck before returning it.

## Anti-patterns that look machine generated
Uniform slide density across the whole deck.
Decorative stock imagery with no informational role.
Gratuitous gradients and shadows.
Icon soup.
Every slide using the same layout.
Generic topic titles such as "Overview", "Benefits", or "Next steps" without a
specific takeaway.
Charts inserted without interpretation.
Large blocks of centered text.
Perfectly balanced but meaningless columns.
Repeated abstract nouns without evidence.

## Output contract
When applying this skill, return the visual system choices, layout assignments,
source status, accessibility status, and unresolved brand questions.
If brand assets are missing, state that the deck uses neutral placeholders and
requires approved brand substitution before external use.
